cc_intro: Compress 13.8 billion years into a 365-day year. January 1 begins with the Big Bang; the present sits exactly at year end. Choose a milestone, then zoom in to see recent history.
cc_year_desc: All markers use the same linear conversion from real years to a 365-day calendar. The orange marker identifies the selected milestone. Orange bands show the selected formation phase or quoted age uncertainty.
cc_year_caption: Recent events cluster at the year’s end. Marker width helps visibility and does not represent an event’s duration.
cc_zoom_desc: Each row has the same time scale. Select an event row with a click, touch, Enter or Space. The cyan interval shows the example lifetime ending at the present.
cc_zoom_visible: The selected milestone is visible in this zoom.
cc_zoom_outside: The selected milestone is earlier than this zoom window. Its position remains on the full-year timeline.
cc_lifetime_help: The cyan interval ends at the present. Choose Second to make it easier to see. Zero years collapses the interval to the end boundary.
cc_formula: Cosmic seconds before year end = years before the present ÷ 13,800,000,000 × 31,536,000. The year has 365 days and February has 28 days. Months have their ordinary, unequal lengths.
cc_precision: The clock shows the arithmetic to hundredths of a cosmic second. Scientific ages remain approximate or carry the quoted uncertainty. The rounded universe age is held fixed; its uncertainty is not propagated. Bands distinguish a formation phase from a dating uncertainty.
cc_data_help: Milestone ages are saved with the simulator and work offline. Each event links to its source. This educational calendar uses a rounded modern age reference; its dates are recalculated rather than copied from an older calendar.
cc_jan1_story: The calendar begins with the hot, dense early universe. Expansion and cooling led to the formation of light elements, and much later, neutral atoms. This scale does not describe the unknown earliest physics.
cc_jan1_basis: Start boundary of the 13.8-billion-year teaching scale.
cc_jan1_source: NASA · Big Bang and the early universe
cc_cmb_story: Around 380,000 years after the Big Bang, electrons and hydrogen nuclei could combine into neutral atoms. Light from this era reaches us as the cosmic microwave background. On this scale, that is about 14.47 minutes after January 1 begins.
cc_cmb_basis: Approximately 380,000 years after the Big Bang; the transition took time.
cc_cmb_source: NASA · Big Bang and the early universe
cc_jan10_story: Gravity drew primordial gas into the earliest stars. Their exact birth dates remain uncertain. The marker uses NASA’s approximate 200-million-year cosmic dawn example; it does not identify a measured first star.
cc_jan10_basis: Illustrative epoch: approximately 200 million years after the Big Bang.
cc_mar15_story: The Milky Way grew through several stages. Xiang and Rix’s 2022 stellar-age study found thick-disk formation beginning about 13 billion years ago, peaking near 11 billion years ago, and continuing until about 8 billion years ago.
cc_mar15_basis: Formation phase: about 13–8 billion years ago. The marker is the approximate 11-billion-year peak. The band is a period of growth.
cc_aug28_story: The Sun and its surrounding disk formed from a collapsing cloud of gas and dust about 4.6 billion years ago. Planets developed within the disk over time. This maps to September 1 on the 365-day scale.
cc_aug28_basis: Approximate formation age: 4.6 billion years ago.
cc_aug28_source: NASA · How our Solar System formed
cc_sep1_story: Djokic and colleagues described biosignatures in ancient hot-spring deposits of Australia’s Dresser Formation. This is one early record of life. A fossil or biosignature dates preserved evidence; it does not establish when life first began.
cc_sep1_basis: Approximate age of the Dresser Formation evidence: 3.48 billion years.
cc_sep1_source: Djokic et al. 2017 · Early life evidence
cc_nov15_story: Javaux, Knoll and Walter described complex eukaryotic microfossils in the Roper Group of northern Australia. These fossils show that features associated with eukaryotic diversification were present by about 1.5 billion years ago. Earlier origins remain a separate question.
cc_nov15_basis: Approximate age of the Roper Group fossil record: 1.5 billion years.
cc_dec5_story: The International Commission on Stratigraphy’s June 2026 chart places the start of the Cambrian at 538.8 ± 0.6 million years ago. Animal diversification extended over time; this geological boundary does not mark the first animal.
cc_dec5_basis: Published boundary age: 538.8 ± 0.6 million years. The band shows the quoted numerical age uncertainty.
cc_dec25_story: Early dinosaur fossils from Argentina and Brazil are about 230 million years old. They are evidence of dinosaurs at that time, rather than an exact date for the group’s origin.
cc_dec25_basis: Approximate fossil age example: 230 million years.
cc_dec31_story: Richter and colleagues dated heated flints associated with the Jebel Irhoud Homo sapiens fossils to 315 ± 34 thousand years. The marker represents this dated archaeological context, rather than a precise birthday for our species.
cc_dec31_basis: Published weighted age: 315 ± 34 thousand years. The band shows the quoted dating uncertainty.
cc_dec31_source: Richter et al. 2017 · Jebel Irhoud dating
cc_agriculture_story: Over roughly the last 12,000 years, people developed farming and herding in multiple places. Different crops and communities changed at different times. The marker is an approximate teaching example of this long transition.
cc_now_story: The present is exactly at the end of this cosmic year: the boundary between December 31 and the next January 1. A lifetime fits into a tiny fraction of the final second. Use the age control to compare that interval.
cc_now_basis: End boundary of the teaching scale: zero seconds remaining.
